description: Map the people at one account who are likely to buy, champion, evaluate or block a purchase in a product category, each with current title, why they matter and a source.
suggested_questions: Map the buying committee at Datadog (datadoghq.com) for a sales engagement platform: economic buyer, champions, evaluators and blockers.
Map who at Brex (brex.com) would buy and evaluate a web data API for their AI agents.
Map the buying committee at Rippling (rippling.com) for a security awareness training product.
skill:
A buying committee is the set of people who decide, influence, evaluate or can block a purchase. For a product
category at one account, find who holds each part of it today.

Roles to map:
- Economic buyer: the executive who owns the budget for the category (often the C-level or VP who owns the function).
- Champions: managers and leaders who own the problem day to day and have spoken or hired around it.
- Technical evaluators: engineering, data, security or operations leaders who would test or approve the product.
- Blockers and gatekeepers: procurement, security, legal or IT leaders, when the category usually needs them.
- Users: the team lead of the people who would use it daily.

Evidence that a person belongs on the map:
- Their title and remit on the company's leadership page, a press release, a speaker page or a current public profile.
- They spoke, wrote or posted about the problem the category solves (cite it).
- They are hiring for the team that would use the product (a job post in their org).
- They were recently appointed (new leaders review vendors; give the start date).

Current role:
- A title is current only when a page dated in the last 12 months shows it, or a profile or company page shows it as the
  present position. Press releases announcing an appointment are dated history: always check for a later change (a
  new title, a departure, a new employer) before calling it current.
- Titles change without a press release: "Chief Revenue Officer" can become "Chief Revenue Architect", "President" or
  "Advisor". Report the title exactly as the newest source states it, with its date.

Pitfalls:
- Org charts are not public. Report reporting lines only when a source states them.
- Do not pad the map. A role you cannot fill from a page is listed in missing_roles.
- Large companies have the same title in several business units or regions: say which one the person covers.

Citations and evidence:
- source_url is one full public https URL: the page the value was read on. Never an internal file path or source id. A
  value from two pages is two values.
- as_of is the date the source states or was published, not today's date.
- A value nobody published is null, listed in missing_fields. Not an estimate from memory.
- Identity drift is the most common error: another person with the same name, a former employee whose old bio is still
  indexed, or a namesake at a similarly named company. Match on name plus company plus title or location before using a
  page.

Privacy:
- Work-related public information only: role, employer, career history, public talks, posts, articles and quotes.
- Never collect home address, personal phone, personal email, family, health, age, religion, politics or other
  sensitive data, and never construct an email or phone number from a pattern. A business email or phone counts only
  when the person or their company published it on a public page for business contact.

why_they_matter.description: One sentence tied to the evidence

evidence.description: What the source shows: a talk, a post, a hiring push, an appointment
